full_judgment:
2. Facts leading to this appeal, in brief, are that the respondent as petitioner filed an application under section 26-F of the Bengal Tenancy Act for pre-empting the suit land; The pre-emption case was contested by the appellant. The trial Court found that the done was a relation by consanguinity within 3 degrees of the donor and as such the gift was exempted from pre-emption in accordance with the provision of section 26-F of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and accordingly dismissed the pre-emption case. On appeal by the pre-emptor, the learned Subordinate Judge affirmed the finding of the learned Munsif and dismissed the appeal. There- after the pre-emptor filed an application under Order 47 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for review of the judgment passed in the Misc. Appeal. The learned Subordinate Judge who dismissed the appeal was in the meanwhile succeeded by another learned Subordinate Judge who heard the review application and allowed the same holding that his predecessor had miscalculated the degree of consanguinity and found that the done did not come within the 3 decrees of consanguinity as provided under the law. Hence the present appeal at the instance of the donee opposite party 

 4. It appears that the trial Court and the lower appellate court had concurrently found that the appellant came within 3 degrees of consanguinity. The learned Subordinate Judge has however, reversed the findings arrived at by the court below but did not assign any reason for the same. He does not say as to how the earlier judgment was wrong nor does he give any basis for his own calculation in arriving at different finding. Be that as it may, even before me the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the parties could not agree on any accepted basis of calculating the 3 degrees of consanguinity as laid down under section 26-F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. In such circumstances when the matter could not be said to be free from or beyond the realm of controversy, I do not see how it could be deemed to be an error apparent on the face of the record. An me which has to be established by along process of reasoning or the point where there may be conceivably two sets of opinion can hardly be called an error apparent on the face of the record, Where an alleged error is far from self evident, and has to be established by lengthy and complicated argument such an error, in my opinion, could not be called an error .apparent the fact of the record. There is, however, distinction between an .erroneous decisions and a decision which could be called an error on the face of the record. A review is by no, means an appeal in disguise whereby an: erroneous decision could be re-heard and corrected. A review lies only fora patent error which is self-evident and which is really apparent on the face of the record. The view I have taken finds support from the Case of Satyanarayan Laxminarayan Mogde and others Vs. Mallidarjun Bhavanappa Tirumalo reported in D.L.R. 1960 (S.C.) page 137. I, therefore, find that the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant has substance.
